name: Reversible infantile respiratory chain deficiency
aliases: Reversible infantile cytochrome c oxidase deficiency

clinicalPearls: A distinctive, spontaneously reversible infantile mitochondrial myopathy most often caused by a homoplasmic point variant in the mitochondrial transfer-RNA-glutamate gene (MT-TE).
It presents in the first weeks to months with profound hypotonia, weakness, feeding difficulty and often respiratory failure requiring ventilatory support, accompanied by lactic acidosis.

Despite a severe, sometimes ventilator-dependent early course, affected infants improve spontaneously, typically from the middle of the first year, and many reach normal or near-normal motor function.
Early muscle biopsy shows severe cytochrome c oxidase (complex IV) deficiency with ragged-red and COX-negative fibres and mitochondrial proliferation, all of which resolve on later biopsy.
Correctly identifying the genotype is crucial because it predicts recovery and should prevent premature withdrawal of intensive or ventilatory support.

A related nuclear-gene disorder, TRMU deficiency, causes a reversible infantile hepatopathy and liver failure; both conditions involve modification or function of mitochondrial transfer-RNA-glutamate.
It must be distinguished from fatal infantile COX-deficiency myopathy (for example SCO2-related disease), which is clinically similar early but non-reversible.
The reversibility is attributed to a developmental increase in expression and aminoacylation of mitochondrial transfer-RNA-glutamate that compensates for the variant over time.
reference.pathophysiology: The disorder is usually due to a homoplasmic point mutation in MT-TE, the gene encoding mitochondrial transfer-RNA-glutamate. Impaired transfer-RNA function limits mitochondrial protein synthesis, so respiratory-chain complexes containing mtDNA-encoded subunits, most conspicuously cytochrome c oxidase, are severely deficient in skeletal muscle during infancy, producing weakness, hypotonia and lactic acidosis. Uniquely, the biochemical defect is transient: a proposed developmental up-regulation of transfer-RNA-glutamate expression, together with improved aminoacylation as the infant matures, progressively restores mitochondrial translation and complex IV activity, mirroring the clinical recovery. In the related TRMU disorder, deficient 2-thiouridylation of mitochondrial transfer RNAs, with cysteine availability acting as a limiting factor, impairs translation chiefly in the liver, again with the capacity for recovery.
additionalDifferentials: Fatal infantile mitochondrial myopathy with COX deficiency (for example SCO2-related, non-reversible)
Congenital myopathies and congenital muscular dystrophies
Congenital myasthenic syndromes and transient neonatal myasthenia
Other mitochondrial DNA or transfer-RNA disorders and depletion syndromes
Pompe disease and other metabolic myopathies
Neonatal sepsis or hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy causing hypotonia
additionalInvestigations: Serial blood lactate and CSF lactate monitoring over time
Muscle biopsy with COX and succinate dehydrogenase histochemistry and respiratory-chain enzymology
Targeted mtDNA testing for the MT-TE transfer-RNA-glutamate variant
Nuclear gene testing including TRMU where hepatopathy predominates
Serial neurophysiology and respiratory function testing as strength recovers
Liver function tests for the TRMU-related hepatic phenotype
Echocardiography and a general mitochondrial disease screen to exclude mimics
redFlags: Neonatal respiratory failure with severe hypotonia and lactic acidosis
Deterioration or failure to improve beyond the expected recovery window, prompting review of the diagnosis
Coexisting acute liver failure suggesting the TRMU phenotype
reference.prognosis: With supportive intensive care through the early critical phase the muscle disorder typically resolves and most children achieve normal or near-normal function; recognising the genotype avoids inappropriate withdrawal of life support.
pitfalls: Withdrawing ventilatory support prematurely by mistaking it for a fatal mitochondrial myopathy.
Failing to test for the MT-TE variant when an infant has a severe but potentially reversible COX-deficient myopathy.
Assuming a single early biopsy reflects the permanent state, when the defect normalises over time.
Confusing the myopathic (MT-TE) and hepatic (TRMU) reversible phenotypes.
Overlooking the role of cysteine as a limiting factor in the TRMU-related hepatopathy.
references: Inborn errors of metabolism reference texts
management: Provide intensive supportive care, including mechanical ventilation, through the early critical phase, recognising the disorder is self-limiting
Confirm the MT-TE genotype so recovery can be predicted and premature withdrawal of ventilatory support avoided
Correct and monitor lactic acidosis with supportive measures and serial blood and CSF lactate
Support nutrition and feeding during the period of profound weakness
Provide physiotherapy and rehabilitation as strength recovers, with serial neurophysiology and respiratory function testing
In the related TRMU disorder, manage the hepatopathy supportively, with cysteine supplementation as proposed
Offer genetic counselling covering the maternally inherited mitochondrial variant or the autosomal recessive TRMU form
